meta.title: PLAID · Your own streaming server, no account, no subscription
meta.description: PLAID turns the drives you already have into a streaming service for the people you love. A self-hosted alternative to Plex: open source, no account, no subscription, nobody watching.

hero.lead: PLAID turns the drives you already have into a streaming service for the people you love: posters, resume where you stopped, an Apple TV app. No account, no subscription, nobody watching.

app.alt: The PLAID web app on a home server: Tears of Steel to continue watching, and a row of recently added films.

what.title: It looks like a streaming service. It belongs to you.

library.title: Your library, made beautiful
library.body: PLAID finds every film and show on your drives, names them, and dresses them in posters, backdrops, cast and trailers. Your files stay exactly where they are.

plays.title: Plays on anything
plays.body: It sends the original file when the screen can play it, and converts only when it can’t, even on a Raspberry Pi. Subtitles, audio tracks and 4K HDR included.

yours.title: Belongs to you
yours.body: Accounts live on your server. No PLAID account, no subscription, no tracking. Open source under MIT.

install.title: Install it
install.body: One line on Ubuntu, Debian or a Raspberry Pi. It runs as a service that starts on boot.

folders.title: Point it at your folders
folders.body: PLAID recognises your films and shows and adds posters, synopses and cast. Your files don’t move.

invite.title: Invite your people
invite.body: Send a link, even to someone far away. The video goes straight from your server to their screen.

vs.title: Private like Jellyfin. Polished like Plex.

account.title: No account with us
account.body: Plex asks everyone to sign in with a Plex account. PLAID has none: accounts live on your server.

looks.title: Looks like a paid service
looks.body: A real home screen, posters and an Apple TV app, built for the people watching, not for the person running the server.

open.title: Open, written from scratch
open.body: Built from the ground up, MIT licensed. No paid tier, no ads, no premium pass.

tv.title: On the TV, it’s a real app.
tv.body: It finds your server on the network, pairs with a short code, and remembers each person: their profile, their language, where they stopped.
tv.alt: The PLAID Apple TV app playing Big Buck Bunny.

points.pins: Profiles with PINs for the kids
points.hdr: 4K HDR and Dolby Atmos, played as they are

party.title: Plaid Party. Everyone lands on the same frame.
party.body: Send one link. Play, pause and seek reach everyone at once, each on a stream made for their screen and their connection.

install.title: One line, before anyone arrives.
install.body: A single Go program with SQLite and FFmpeg. The script installs it as a service that starts on boot. No Docker needed, though it works there too.
install.note: Ubuntu, Debian · amd64 and arm64 · Raspberry Pi 4 or 5

account.title: Lives on your server.
account.body: The first visit creates the admin account on your machine. There is nothing to sign up for with us.

remote.title: Send a link, not instructions.
remote.body: Turn on remote access and your server gets an address with a real certificate. Video goes straight from you to them.

free.a: Yes. It’s open source under the MIT licence, with no subscription and no paid tier.

account.q: Do I need a PLAID account?
account.a: No. The first visit creates the admin account on your own server. Nothing is sent to us.

pi.q: Will it run on my Raspberry Pi?
pi.a: A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with a 64-bit system is enough for a family. Any amd64 or arm64 Linux machine works.

video.q: Where does the video go when friends watch from home?
video.a: Straight from your server to them. getplaid.direct only gives your server an address with a certificate.

party.a: Its intent is written; the spec comes next, then the code. Follow the roadmap on GitHub.

meta.title: Features · PLAID
meta.description: What PLAID does today and what is planned: libraries, artwork, Direct Play and transcoding, web and Apple TV apps, accounts, remote access.

features.title: Everything it does. Nothing it pretends to.
features.lead: PLAID runs on your own hardware. Each feature says where it stands.
features.bannerAlt: Big Buck Bunny in a sunny forest clearing.

scan.name: Folder scanning
scan.body: New files show up on their own. Network shares are rescanned every 15 minutes. PLAID only reads your folders.

match.name: Matching and artwork
match.body: Titles, posters and synopses from TMDB and fanart.tv, in each library’s language. Your own .nfo files and images win.

search.name: Search and collections
search.body: Find a film, a show or a person, and browse collections.

direct.name: Direct Play
direct.body: When a screen can play the file as it is, PLAID sends it untouched, using almost no CPU.

transcode.name: Direct Stream and transcoding
transcode.body: When it can’t, PLAID remuxes or re-encodes to H.264 with FFmpeg, at a quality that fits the connection.

hardware.name: Hardware transcoding
hardware.body: VAAPI, Intel Quick Sync, NVENC and V4L2 M2M, tested at startup, with software as the fallback.

subtitles.name: Subtitles
subtitles.body: Text and image subtitles. Each profile’s audio and subtitle choices are remembered.

resume.name: Continue watching
resume.body: Stop on one screen, pick up on another. Each profile keeps its place.

web.name: Web
web.body: Served by the server itself, in any recent browser.

appletv.name: Apple TV
appletv.body: A native tvOS app that finds the server and pairs with a code.

ios.name: iPhone and iPad
ios.body: SwiftUI, right after the Apple TV app.

android.name: Android and Android TV
android.body: Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, after the Apple apps.

accounts.name: Accounts and profiles
accounts.body: An admin, members, and a profile per person, with an optional PIN.

pairing.name: TV pairing
pairing.body: A TV signs in with a short code typed on another device.

remote.name: Remote access
remote.body: A getplaid.direct address and a real certificate for your server.

sharing.name: Library sharing
sharing.body: Invite someone by link to one library or collection, with a quality cap and instant revocation.

party.name: Plaid Party
party.body: Watch together, in sync, from different homes.

features.legend: **Available** means merged and in the releases. **Planned** means the intent is written. **Later** means it waits its turn.

meta.title: Plaid Party · Watch together, in sync · PLAID
meta.description: Plaid Party keeps everyone on the same frame, wherever they are and whatever they watch on. Planned: the intent is written, the spec is next.

party.title: Same film. Same second. Different couches.
party.lead: A Plaid Party keeps everyone on the same frame, wherever they are and whatever they watch on.
party.bannerAlt: Count Orlok in a doorway, in Nosferatu (1922).

start.title: Start a party
start.body: Pick a film and choose Plaid Party. You get a link and a short code to send.

join.title: Everyone’s here
join.body: Friends join from a TV, a laptop or a phone. You see who is watching and who is still loading.

play.title: Press play once
play.body: Play, pause and seek reach everyone together, less than half a second apart.

streams.title: 4K on the TV, 720p on the train
streams.body: Each screen gets its own stream. The TV plays the file as it is; the phone on mobile data gets a lighter one. Nobody waits for the slowest.

drift.title: No “wait, where are you?”
drift.body: The server keeps the shared clock. If someone drifts, their speed adjusts gently instead of jumping. After buffering, they slip back in.

pause.title: Sam asks for a pause
pause.body: Anyone can ask. The host decides, or everyone votes.

room.alt: Concept of a Plaid Party room on Nosferatu at 1:12:48: Sam on an Apple TV in 4K Direct Play, Mia on an iPad in 1080p, Léo on a phone on a train in 720p, Alex on a laptop in Direct Play.
room.caption: Concept, drawn with the PLAID design system. Nosferatu (1922), public domain.

reactions.title: Reactions
reactions.body: Emoji that float over the picture, for everyone.

chat.title: Chat
chat.body: A side panel that never covers the film.

requests.title: Pause requests
requests.body: A gentle nudge to the host, or to everyone.

control.title: Who controls
control.body: The host only, or everyone. Switch any time.

notv1.title: Not in version 1: video and voice chat.
notv1.body: You probably have a call open already. PLAID keeps the picture for the film.

meta.title: Install · PLAID
meta.description: Install PLAID in a minute on Ubuntu, Debian or Docker, on amd64 or arm64: one script, a Debian package or Docker Compose.

install.title: Install PLAID in a minute.
install.lead: Ubuntu, Debian or Docker, on amd64 or arm64. Every way ends the same: open your server in a browser.
install.bannerAlt: Two characters argue on a bridge over an Amsterdam canal, in Tears of Steel.

script.name: Script
script.body: Installs PLAID as a service that starts on boot, on Ubuntu or Debian. It checks the package checksum before installing. [**Read the script first.**]({script})

deb.name: Debian package
deb.body: Download `plaid_<version>_amd64.deb` (or arm64) and `checksums.txt` from the [latest release]({releases}), then:

files.service: Enabled and started, runs as the plaid user

docker.name: Docker
docker.body: Clone the repository and start it. Mount your media folders read-only in `docker-compose.yml`, then use the container paths when you add a library.

open.title: Open it
open.body: Visit your server on port 32500. The first run creates the admin account, adds folders and picks their language. From outside your network, PLAID asks for the setup code printed in its log.

folders.title: Point it at your folders
folders.body: Add movie and show libraries, each with its own language. PLAID scans, matches and fetches artwork. It never changes your media. The package runs as the plaid user, which can’t read your home folder until you allow it.

systems.name: Systems
systems.value: Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 LTS, Debian 12 and later

arch.name: Processors
arch.value: amd64 (most PCs), arm64 (Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 on a 64-bit system, ARM servers)

meta.title: Remote access with getplaid.direct · PLAID
meta.description: Turn on remote access and your PLAID server gets an address with a real certificate. Video never passes through getplaid.direct.

remote.title: Your server, reachable from anywhere.
remote.lead: Turn it on in Settings, Remote access. Your server gets an address with a real certificate, and video never passes through getplaid.direct.
remote.bannerAlt: A young man rests among scrap robots, in Tears of Steel.

steps.label: How it works, in four steps

port.title: Open a port
port.body: PLAID asks your router with UPnP or NAT-PMP. If that fails, choose Manual and forward a TCP port to 32501 on the PLAID machine.

name.title: Get a name
name.body: PLAID registers with getplaid.direct and gets a name that points to your public IP. It follows your IP when it changes; the server checks in every 15 minutes.

cert.title: Get a certificate
cert.body: A Let’s Encrypt certificate for that name, through a DNS challenge. No port 80, and the private key stays on your server.

link.title: Send the link
link.body: A short getplaid.direct link that leads to your server. Before you share it, getplaid.direct checks from outside that your server answers.

never.title: Video never goes through us.
never.body: After one redirect and a DNS answer that gives your home IP, screens connect straight to your server. Behind CGNAT this can’t work; use a VPN instead.

friend.title: Your friend
friend.body: Opens the link in a browser or on Apple TV.

direct.title: getplaid.direct
direct.body: Answers one DNS question and one redirect. Nothing else.

server.title: Your server
server.body: Streams the film straight to your friend.

off.title: Turn it off, and it’s gone.
off.body: Switching it off deletes your server’s records at once. A server that hasn’t checked in for 30 days is removed too.

cgnat.title: CGNAT
cgnat.body: Some providers share one public IP between homes, so no port can open. Use Tailscale or a similar VPN.

docker.title: Docker
docker.body: UPnP can’t see your router from Docker’s default network. Use `network_mode: host`, or choose Manual and publish `32501:32501`.

own.title: Your own setup
own.body: Your own domain, reverse proxy or tunnel works with getplaid.direct turned off.

meta.title: The getplaid.direct protocol · PLAID
meta.description: Everything getplaid.direct does fits on one page: names, seven HTTP calls, short links, DNS answers and the rules a PLAID server can rely on.

protocol.title: The protocol, in the open.
protocol.lead: Everything getplaid.direct does fits on one page: give your server a name, help it get a certificate, redirect one link. Version 1.

names.title: Three kinds of names, one per server.
names.body: The label is the server name made safe for DNS, cut to 20 characters, plus 6 random characters. The random part alone identifies the server.

rows.public: Your server’s public IP. This is the address friends use.
rows.lan: A private address on your network, so screens at home stay at home.
rows.acme: Set by your server while it gets its own certificate.

api.title: Seven calls, JSON in and out.
api.body: Base URL `{base}`. Errors come back as a code and an English sentence, with a 4xx or 5xx status.

calls.register: Register. Returns the id, a secret token shown once, the hostname and the short link. 5 per IP per hour.
calls.update: Update and heartbeat: at startup, every 15 minutes, and when the port changes.
calls.acmeSet: Set the DNS-01 values for a certificate. They expire after 1 hour.
calls.reach: Check from outside that a PLAID server answers. 10 per server per hour.
calls.ip: The address the service sees for you. No token needed.

links.title: One link to remember.
links.note: The redirect is all the service does. An old name still redirects, to the current one. Port 443 is left out of the address.

dns.title: The service answers for getplaid.direct.
dns.body: It is the zone’s authoritative name server, not a resolver: questions about other zones are refused, unknown names are NXDOMAIN.

rows.label: Your server’s last public IPv4 / IPv6
rows.lan: a.b.c.d, only for private, CGNAT and link-local ranges

rules.title: Details a server can rely on.

source.title: The address is the request’s
source.body: Your public IP is always the source of the call. Nobody can point a name at an address they don’t own.

families.title: IPv4 and IPv6 apart
families.body: A call refreshes only its own family. An address not refreshed for 24 hours stops being published.

token.title: One token, one server
token.body: Every call after registering carries a bearer token. A wrong token and an unknown id get the same 401.

ttl.title: Short TTLs
ttl.body: 60 seconds for server records, so a new home IP spreads fast. Servers silent for 30 days are removed.

keys.title: Keys stay home
keys.body: Each server gets its own Let’s Encrypt certificate through DNS-01. The private key never leaves your machine.

probe.title: No probing inside
probe.body: The reachability check never connects to a private, CGNAT or link-local address.

read.title: Read the whole document.
read.body: PROTOCOL.md lives next to the service’s code, versioned with it.

meta.title: FAQ · PLAID
meta.description: Questions about PLAID, answered plainly: price, accounts, your data, Raspberry Pi, Docker, and watching with friends.

faq.title: Questions, answered plainly.
faq.lead: If yours isn’t here, ask it on GitHub. We answer.
faq.bannerAlt: A llama stares in surprise, in Caminandes.

free.a: Yes. Open source under MIT, with no paid tier. It will stay that way.

today.a: Yes, though it’s early. The server, the web app and the Apple TV app handle libraries, artwork, playback and remote access. Sharing and Plaid Party are coming; expect rough edges.

fork.q: Is it a Plex or Jellyfin fork?
fork.a: No. PLAID is written from scratch, with its own API and apps.

account.q: Does PLAID need an online account?
account.a: No. Accounts live on your server. The project asks nothing of you.

sends.q: Does it send anything to you?
sends.a: No telemetry. Your server asks TMDB and fanart.tv for posters and synopses, sending only titles, years and IDs, never what you watch. With remote access on, getplaid.direct learns your public IP and port.

files.a: Exactly where they are. PLAID reads your folders and never moves or changes your media.

pi.q: Will it run on a Raspberry Pi?
pi.a: Yes, a Pi 4 or 5 on a 64-bit system. Direct Play costs almost nothing; converting on a Pi is done in software, so a machine with a GPU does much better for files your screens can’t play as they are.

docker.a: No. The Debian package installs a normal system service. Docker works too.

reach.q: How do friends reach my server from outside?
reach.a: Turn on remote access for a getplaid.direct address and a real certificate, use your own reverse proxy, or a tunnel like Tailscale or Cloudflare Tunnel.

install.q: Do my friends need to install anything?
install.a: No. A browser is enough. On Apple TV there’s an app.

meta.title: Privacy · PLAID
meta.description: What getplaid.direct keeps, and for how long: almost nothing, and only if you turn remote access on. This website keeps nothing at all.

privacy.title: What we keep, and for how long.
privacy.lead: Short answer: almost nothing, and only if you turn remote access on. This website keeps nothing at all.
privacy.bannerAlt: A close-up of Big Buck Bunny holding a twig.

kept.title: What getplaid.direct stores
kept.body: Only after you turn remote access on, and only per server.

token.name: Token
token.value: A SHA-256 hash of the server’s secret token, never the token

port.name: Port
port.value: The external port your router forwards

dates.name: Dates
dates.value: When the server registered and was last seen

acme.name: Challenges
acme.value: Temporary DNS values while a certificate is issued, gone after an hour

never.title: Your films, your libraries, your accounts, what you watch.
never.body: Video goes straight from your server to the screen. getplaid.direct only answers DNS.

gone.title: The moment you turn it off.
gone.body: Or on its own after 30 days without hearing from your server.

server.title: No telemetry.
server.body: To match your films it sends titles, years and IDs to TMDB and fanart.tv, with your server’s IP. Never accounts or what you watch.

site.title: Nothing about you.
site.body: No analytics, cookies, third-party scripts or fonts. Nothing is stored in your browser.

questions.title: Ask on GitHub.
questions.body: The service’s behaviour is written in its [protocol document]({protocol}), in the open.
